implementation_notes: Modern JavaScript times a call out by aborting it: AbortSignal.timeout(ms) returns a signal that aborts with a TimeoutError DOMException, which fetch, streams and Node's HTTP APIs accept through their signal option, and AbortSignal.any([userSignal, timeoutSignal]) merges the deadline with the caller's own cancellation so one signal carries both. The timer counts active time (it is paused in a suspended worker or a page in the back/forward cache) and cannot be cancelled early, and while the timeout is pending the signal is kept alive if abort listeners are attached; when the operation can finish early, AbortController plus setTimeout/clearTimeout is the more precise tool.
pitfalls: The signal only works because the callee honours it: a library that ignores the signal option, or a callback API, never aborts and needs its own timer.

AbortSignal.timeout() cannot be cancelled early and its timer keeps the signal alive while abort listeners are attached, so long budgets in hot paths pin memory - use AbortController + clearTimeout there.
Distinguishing TimeoutError from AbortError is part of the contract: a caller cancellation must not be retried or reported as a dependency timeout.
Node is single-threaded, so a call that never times out holds an in-flight slot and its sockets rather than a thread - the capacity leak is still real.

variants.name: Promise.race against a timer (pre-AbortSignal, manual)
variants.implementation_notes: The portable realization races the operation against a timer promise that rejects after the budget: it needs no platform support and works with APIs that accept no signal, but it stops only the await. The losing promise keeps running, its later rejection can surface as an unhandled rejection, and any timer that is not cleared keeps the event loop alive - which is why this variant is a fallback and not the default. It remains the correct choice for wrapping a third-party promise-returning function that cannot be cancelled, and it should still forward an AbortSignal to the underlying client wherever one is accepted.
pitfalls: The operation keeps running after the race: without an AbortSignal the request, its sockets and its buffers outlive the caller's interest.
A promise that rejects after it lost the race becomes an unhandled rejection unless a catch is attached before racing.
setTimeout resolution is not a deadline: under event-loop pressure the timer can fire later than requested, so the bound is approximate.
